node.label: Bettina Bradbury
node.date_label: Working Families (1993) · Negotiating Identities, with Tamara Myers (2005) · Wife to Widow (2011)
node.description: In Working Families (1993), Bettina Bradbury argues that Montreal working-class survival depended on children's earnings and women's unpaid work as well as men's wages. She treats the household as a place of support and inequality, linking class formation to age, gender and the family life cycle. Joan Sangster credits her family-economy studies with helping recast working-class history; Cynthia Comacchio praises the integration of class and gender but questions how historians can distinguish deliberate family strategies from emergency coping. Wife to Widow (2011) follows women's transition into widowhood through law, property, religion and politics. With Tamara Myers, she also framed Negotiating Identities (2005) around the spaces between formal politics and family life.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Canadian Family History: Selected Readings (1992, editor); Working Families: Age, Gender, and Daily Survival in Industrializing Montreal (1993); Familles ouvrières à Montréal (1995, translated by Christiane Teasdale); Negotiating Identities in Nineteenth- and Twentieth-Century Montreal (2005, co-edited with Tamara Myers); Wife to Widow: Lives, Laws, and Politics in Nineteenth-Century Montreal (2011).
node.scope_note: Working Families read in a licensed 2007 preview: imprint, acknowledgments and introduction pp. 13–18; later displayed passages consulted, not the full book. The 1987 and 2000 essays and Comacchio's review read selectively at the locators recorded below. Negotiating Identities read in publisher front matter and selected introductory passages and notes, not all chapters. Wife to Widow and Canadian Family History unread in full; claims about them rest on publisher description or a named reviewer. Burgess's review body and Bradbury's 1980 Tilly–Scott review unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Women's History and Working-Class History” (1987), Bradbury faults Kealey and Palmer's Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) for discounting wives' domestic labour when interpreting skilled men's ideal wife.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 35–36, nn. 59, 61–62: “crude moralizing”; qualified criticism of both coauthors. Dreaming itself unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Domestic labour and skilled men's pride

proposed_edges.relationship: Bradbury's “Women's History and Working-Class History” (1987) challenges Palmer and Kealey's reading of the ideal wife in Dreaming of What Might Be (1982).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 35–36, nn. 59, 61–62: she stresses domestic work and acknowledges their point about women's sphere. Coauthored original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bradbury commends Parr's “Hired Men” (1985) in “Women's History and Working-Class History” (1987) for integrating family into labour history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 39, n. 74: “change and improve it”; shared praise with Greer. Parr's original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bradbury commends Greer's “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism” (1985) in her 1987 essay for integrating family into labour history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 39, n. 74: praise alongside Parr, not sole derivation. Greer's original unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Family in the transition to capitalism

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History” (2000), Sangster credits Bradbury's family-economy studies (1979–1984) with having contributed “immensely to a recasting of working-class history”, and recalls Bradbury's 1987 charge that efforts to integrate women into working-class history remained circumscribed.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 140, nn. 46–47: “contributed immensely to a recasting”. The note identifies studies from 1979, 1982 and 1984; the appraisal is Sangster's, not a claim that all her work derives from Bradbury. Only selected passages of the 2000 essay read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beneath the ‘Sentimental Veil’” (1994), Comacchio praises Working Families (1993) but questions whether observed coping practices establish deliberate family strategies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 287–288: “basic problem of definition” and “reactive, ad hoc, emergency coping measures”; p. 280 supplies praise. Specific methodological reservation, not rejection of the book; selected review passages read, monograph only in preview.
proposed_edges.map_label: How can historians establish family strategies?

proposed_edges.relationship: Working Families (1993) places women's unpaid work and children's earnings alongside men's wages in explaining working-class survival during Montreal's industrialization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 14–16 read in 2007 preview: “beyond the factory and workshop”. Later chapters unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Family work beyond the male wage

proposed_edges.relationship: Wife to Widow (2011) connects women's transitions into widowhood with law, property, religion and politics in nineteenth-century Montreal.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UBC Press description and contents read: “shifting conditions of patriarchy”. Publisher account only; 2011 book unread. The linked sample actually contains Negotiating Identities (2005).

proposed_edges.relationship: Comacchio's 1994 review presents Canadian Family History (1992) and Working Families (1993) as contributions to understanding family life through class, gender and age.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 280: “differential experience of family”. This is the named reviewer's assessment; the 1992 reader unread and the monograph read only in preview.
proposed_edges.map_label: Age and gender in family history

proposed_edges.relationship: In their introduction to Negotiating Identities (2005), Bradbury and Tamara Myers connect studies of regulation and identity to McKay's liberal-order programme (2000).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 7–8, p. 20 n. 25: “class power beyond the realm of the economic”. Collective framing, not an endorsement of every McKay claim. Other chapters unread; distinct from the existing roster's comparison of Working Families.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fahrni's 2014 scholarly tribute credits Working Families (1993) with transforming understandings of the Industrial Revolution in Quebec and Canada.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Fahrni's full introduction, pp. 267–269, especially p. 267: “transformed our understanding”. Named reception claim; not a fresh reading of the whole monograph.
proposed_edges.map_label: A feminist family history of Quebec industrialization

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Importance of Being Monogamous (2008), Sarah Carter draws on Bettina Bradbury’s “Colonial Comparisons: Rethinking Marriage, Civilization and Nation in Nineteenth-Century White Settler Societies” (2005) to frame marriage laws as claims to colonial civilization and instruments of settler identity in Western Canada.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s chapter 1 and its notes. Carter names and quotes Bradbury in the body, then relates the argument to Western Canada. Notes 9–10 identify the 2005 chapter, pp. 150 and 136. This is substantive uptake rather than a citation-only association; no claim of supervision.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bettina Bradbury’s Working Families (1993) contributed to family history by using the household economy to connect women’s subsistence work with family survival, an approach Mary Anne Poutanen (2014) identifies as foundational and applies to residential prostitution and tavern-keeping.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete journal contribution. Poutanen explains the book’s method and describes her own applications in the body. The target includes history of the family: this edge does not claim a demographic technique or dataset. Poutanen is absent from both eligible endpoint lists, so her specific debt is evidence for the field contribution, not a proposed person edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Household economy as a family-history method

proposed_edges.relationship: Bettina Bradbury’s “Colonial Comparisons: Rethinking Marriage, Civilization and Nation in Nineteenth-Century White Settler Societies” (2005) contributed to comparative settler-colonial history by examining how marriage regimes marked colonial difference and preserved white male authority across settler societies, as assessed by Jarett Henderson (2014).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete journal contribution. Henderson explains the comparison across Canada, New Zealand, Australia and the Cape and explicitly assesses its methodological contribution. The edge concerns published historical analysis, without reproducing oral narratives or community knowledge. Henderson is absent from the eligible endpoint lists.
proposed_edges.map_label: Marriage regimes in comparative colonial history
